title: Deep sleep's embrace
hook: the best night's sleep you ever had, with nothing in it, and something that still woke up rested
carry: in deep sleep, the self is still there
tomorrow: death — the caterpillar reaching the next blade

segments.voice: Yesterday: dreaming. No chariots there, and the dreamer makes them, lit by the self. Your line was the self lights even your dreams.

Some nights you sleep so deeply there's nothing to report. No dream, no time passing, no you. Then the alarm, and you sit up and say, I slept like a stone. It's the best sleep there is, and nobody was there to enjoy it. Or was there? Who, exactly, slept well? Yajnavalkya takes King Janaka one floor below the dreams, to the place you go every night and never remember.
screen: `NOTHING TO REPORT.` → `I SLEPT LIKE A STONE.` → `WHO SLEPT WELL?`

segments.voice: As a falcon or an eagle, Yajnavalkya says, tired from circling all day in the sky, folds its wings and heads home to its nest, so a person hurries to that state where, asleep, he wants nothing and sees no dream. Then the image this day is named for. As a man held by the one he loves knows nothing outside and nothing inside, so a person held by the knowing self knows nothing outside and nothing inside. That is the form, the text says, where every desire is met, so there's no desire at all, and no sorrow. Then a startling list. There, a father is not a father, a mother not a mother. Gods are not gods. A thief is not a thief. Untouched by good, untouched by evil, he has crossed every sorrow of the heart. Nothing you are in daylight follows you in. And yet the text insists this isn't a blank. When he doesn't see there, he is still seeing, for the seer's seeing is never lost. There's just no second thing to see. Vedanta teachers draw a famous clue from this. You wake up and say, I slept well; I knew nothing. Who knew it was good? Someone was there: the self, resting with no roles at all. Not a daughter, not a student, not a worrier. That's the teaching: you are not your roles; the self is there even when every role is gone. In the Chandogya, Indra feared deep sleep was like being destroyed; here Yajnavalkya calls it an embrace. The Mandukya, which you met last year, names this state prajna, the third of the self's four quarters.
screen: `THE FALCON FOLDS ITS WINGS.` · `HELD, KNOWING NOTHING OUTSIDE OR IN.` · `A FATHER IS NOT A FATHER.` · `I SLEPT WELL. WHO KNEW?` · then, large: `IN DEEP SLEEP, THE SELF IS STILL THERE.`

segments.voice: Picture the falcon, tired, circling lower and lower, and with each out-breath fold something in: your plans for tonight, your name, your job, the role you play for other people. You're not trying to fall asleep, only letting the day's sky go, and resting in the nest with nothing outside to watch and nothing inside to fix.
Deep sleep. No dream, no desire, no sorrow: a person held by prajna, the knowing self, with nothing outside and nothing inside. In the Mandukya, the third state.
Your line: in deep sleep, the self is still there. The seer's seeing is never lost. Sleep well.

howItsDone: Vedanta teachers use deep sleep, described here and in the Mandukya Upanishad, as an everyday clue to the self: something rests, and on waking, one knows one slept well.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): the word segment presented 'prajna' as today's word instead of the index word, so it didn't match the say-it and rhythm games; it now names 'deep sleep' and keeps prajna inside.
The embrace image (4.3.21) is in the text as a man embraced by a beloved wife; the script renders it as 'held by the one he loves'. Confirm this is acceptable.
The list in 4.3.22 also includes the outcaste and the murderer; the script gives a selection.
'The seer's seeing is never lost' paraphrases 4.3.23 (na hi draṣṭur dṛṣṭer viparilopo vidyate).
